_comment: Held-out set for US-55 (#346). Each record is one real F-1 finding, generated live from the real pipeline against tests/fixtures/rtr-us5-insecure and tests/fixtures/rtr-us5-messy, one captured explanation (ai/explain.py, real Ollama call), and independent human ratings on the same 1-5 scale docs/evaluation.md Part 3 uses. 'Held out' means these five findings are not among ai/Modelfile's own worked examples (checked: none of their IDs or exact text appear there). Captured 2026-10-10, after #145's fix landed, specifically to measure current behaviour rather than reuse docs/evaluation.md's pre-#145 text. See docs/evaluation.md Part 4 for the full writeup, including the AC-002 defect this honestly includes rather than re-rolls away.

rating_scale.accuracy: 1 (poor) to 5 (excellent) -- does the text claim only what the finding's own evidence actually shows
rating_scale.usefulness: 1 (poor) to 5 (excellent) -- would this sentence, alone, tell someone who has never read evidence.detail what is actually wrong

captured_against._comment: What produced every model-written explanation below. If ai/Modelfile's sha256 no longer matches this, the set is stale: re-capture and re-rate rather than editing the ratings in place (#346 review, @ARSH871-bot).

finding.summary: 2 route assertion(s) could not be checked against this config

evidence.detail: They are written about rtr-branch, rtr-hq, which are not in this snapshot. Nothing is claimed about them either way.

findings.captured_explanation: This check could not be completed, so nothing is confirmed about the network either way. The underlying reason: They are written about rtr-branch, rtr-hq, which are not in this snapshot. Nothing is claimed about them either way.

ratings.notes: Deterministic fallback, so accuracy cannot be wrong by construction. Usefulness is slightly mechanical -- it restates evidence.detail almost verbatim -- but that is exactly what a safe fallback is supposed to do, and it names the two affected devices plainly.

finding.summary: Unencrypted web traffic reaches the internal server

evidence.detail: Expected DENY but got PERMIT, decided by: permit ip any any

findings.captured_explanation: The device's current configuration allows unencrypted web traffic to reach the internal server. This is in conflict with the policy requirement that should block such traffic, which is currently set to DENY. The reason for this discrepancy lies in the device's own configuration, specifically its rule allowing all incoming traffic without restriction.

ratings.notes: Correctly attributes the problem to the device's own permit-any-any rule, and correctly states the requirement is DENY. No inversion. Slightly repetitive across its three sentences rather than genuinely re-explained.

finding.summary: The internal network can reach servers it should not

evidence.detail: Flow start=rtr-us5 [10.10.10.0:49152->8.8.8.8:80 TCP (SYN)] is permitted but policy requires it to be DENIED. Decided by: permit ip any any [Rules checked: Netwise's built-in example policy (analysis/checks/policy_compliance.py) -- no policy file was supplied.]

findings.captured_explanation: The internal network can reach servers it should not, specifically the server at 8.8.8.8 on port 80, due to a configuration allowing unencrypted web traffic through despite policy requirements blocking it. The device's own configuration is permitting this traffic, which contradicts its written policy that forbids it.

ratings.notes: This is one of the two findings #145 was filed against (the pre-#145 text here scored 4/3, 2/3, 2/2, 2/2 across the four raters in docs/evaluation.md Part 3, because the old text said 'the policy currently permits this unauthorized access' -- backwards). Regenerated after the fix: now correctly says the device permits traffic 'despite policy requirements blocking it' and that the config 'contradicts its written policy that forbids it'. The inversion is gone. Names the exact destination (8.8.8.8:80), which the old text also did.

finding.summary: ACL rule never takes effect in acl_in

evidence.detail: Unreachable line: permit udp 10.10.10.0 0.0.0.255 host 218.8.104.58 eq domain (action PERMIT). Blocked by: deny   ip 10.10.10.0 0.0.0.255 any. Reason: BLOCKING_LINES

findings.captured_explanation: The device's access control rule for traffic from the internal network (10.10.10.0/24) to a specific host (218.8.104.58) is never enforced, despite being set to allow it. The reason for this is that an earlier rule blocks all traffic from the same source IP address to any destination. As a result, even though the rule itself permits the desired traffic, it is effectively overridden by the blocking rule, and no traffic reaches its intended destination.

ratings.notes: RE-CAPTURED a fourth time (9 November), after review found naming the blocking line in raw ACL syntax (the 5 November fix) measurably traded that misdescription for a different one: 30 live generations went from 0/30 calling the dead PERMIT line a block to 16/30 calling the /24 source a specific host. Fixed by describing the blocking line in plain English instead of raw syntax (_describe_acl_line()), refusing rather than guessing on any shape it does not recognise. Re-measured, same finding, 30 generations: 0/30 call the PERMIT line a block, 1/30 clearly calls the source a specific host (down from 16/30), 1/30 ambiguous, 0/30 copy Modelfile Example 1 verbatim. This capture states both source and destination explicitly and correctly, names the real cause (an earlier deny rule), and invents nothing beyond the evidence. Two things found along the way, reported but out of scope for this fix: 2/30 invert the flow direction (says traffic runs from the destination to the source), 2/30 echo Example 1's "unencrypted" vocabulary without copying the phrase exactly -- filed as follow-up observations, not fixed here. @ARSH871-bot @shubhamkataria2005, fresh capture against a changed fact -- please rate again.

finding.summary: HTTPS to the internal server is blocked, so the service is unreachable

evidence.detail: Flow start=rtr-us5 [10.10.10.0:49152->10.20.0.5:443 TCP (SYN)] is denied but policy requires it to be PERMITTED. Decided by: deny   ip 10.10.10.0 0.0.0.255 any [Rules checked: Netwise's built-in example policy (analysis/checks/policy_compliance.py) -- no policy file was supplied.]

findings.captured_explanation: The internal server can be reached over HTTPS traffic, but the device's configuration blocks it. The written policy actually requires this traffic to be allowed, so the blockage is due to the device's own configuration rather than the policy itself. As a result, the service remains unreachable because the required traffic is being denied by the device's rules.

ratings.notes: This is the other finding #145 was filed against -- the pre-#145 text scored 3/2, 1/2, 1/2, 1/2 across the four raters, because it said 'a specific policy statement that requires blocking of HTTPS traffic', the opposite of the evidence. Regenerated after the fix: now correctly says the device's configuration blocks it and the policy 'requires this traffic to be allowed'. The inversion is gone -- accuracy moves from the old mean of 1.5 to 5. Usefulness held at 3, not higher: the first sentence ('can be reached over HTTPS... but blocks it') still asks the reader to resolve an apparent contradiction before the next two sentences clarify it, the same readability risk multiple raters flagged on the old text, now just no longer paired with a false claim underneath it.
